{{Short description|Theorem in condensed matter physics}}
[[Image:Fermi Surface.svg|thumb|200 px|right|Luttinger's theorem relates a Fermi liquid's particle density to the volume of its Fermi surface.]]

In [[condensed matter physics]], '''Luttinger's theorem'''<ref>
{{Cite journal
|author1=Luttinger, J. M. |author2=Ward, J. C. | year = 1960
| title = Ground-State Energy of a Many-Fermion System. II
| journal = [[Physical Review]]
| volume = 118 | issue = 5 | pages = 1417–1427
| doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.118.1417
|bibcode = 1960PhRv..118.1417L }}</ref><ref>
{{Cite journal
| last = Luttinger | first = J. M.
| year = 1960
| title = Fermi Surface and Some Simple Equilibrium Properties of a System of Interacting Fermions
| journal = [[Physical Review]]
| volume = 119 | issue = 4 | pages = 1153–1163
| doi =  10.1103/PhysRev.119.1153
|bibcode = 1960PhRv..119.1153L }}</ref> is a result derived by [[Joaquin Mazdak Luttinger|J. M. Luttinger]] and [[John Clive Ward|J. C. Ward]] in 1960 that has broad implications in the field of [[electron]] transport. It arises frequently in theoretical models of correlated electrons, such as the [[high-temperature superconductivity|high-temperature superconductor]]s, and in [[photoemission]], where a metal's [[Fermi surface]] can be directly observed.

==Definition==

Luttinger's theorem states that '''the volume enclosed by a material's Fermi surface is directly proportional to the particle density'''.

While the theorem is an immediate result of the [[Pauli exclusion principle]] in the case of noninteracting particles, it remains true even as interactions between particles are taken into consideration provided that the appropriate definitions of Fermi surface and particle density are adopted. Specifically, in the interacting case the Fermi surface must be defined according to the criteria that
:<math>G(\omega=0,\,p) \to 0</math>   or   <math>\infty,</math>
where <math>G</math> is the single-particle [[Green's function|Green function]] in terms of [[frequency]] and [[momentum]]. Then Luttinger's theorem can be recast into the form<ref>
{{cite book 
 | author = Abrikosov, A. A., Gorkov, L. P. and Dzyaloshinsky, I. E. 
 | year = 1963
 | title = Methods of Quantum Field Theory in Statistical Physics
 | edition=revised | page = 168
 | publisher = Dover, New York
}}</ref>
:<math>n = 2 \int_{\mathcal{Re\,}G(\omega=0,k)>0}\frac{d^D k}{(2\pi)^D}</math>,
where <math>\mathcal{Re\,}G</math> is the real part of the above [[Green's function|Green function]] and <math>d^D k</math> is the differential volume of <math>k</math>-space in <math>D</math> dimensions.
